Fallacy: "It's always been this way"

t: Ad hominem and poisoning the well
s: Fallacy: Attacking the person
Fallacy: Linking the idea to something hated
Fallacy: "There are more important things"
Fallacy: One case against the data
Fallacy: Selecting only the favorable data
Fallacy: The truth is always in the middle
Fallacy: Swapping "is it wrong?" for another question
Bias: Loving animals and eating them creates tension, resolved by denying minds to the animals eaten (Bastian et al., 2012)
Bias: Looking for reasons for the conclusion you already want
Bias: Accepting only what confirms a prior belief
Bias: Preferring the current state because it is current
Bias: Legitimizing the existing order to reduce discomfort
Bias: Avoiding information that would create an obligation
Bias: "Food" animals are granted less mind than "pet" animals
Bias: Valuing "our own" and devaluing outsiders
Bias: Billions of victims don't weigh more than one
Bias: Shared blame feels like no blame
Bias: Pushing back when freedom feels threatened
Bias: Rejecting ideas that threaten the group or one's identity
Bias: "I like it, so it's good"
Bias: One good act licenses a bad one
Bias: "My meat is different"
Bias: We only see those who made it
Bias: Justifying eating animals by saying it is natural, normal, necessary and nice (Piazza and colleagues, 2015).
Bias: Looking for an inconsistency in whoever defends an idea so as not to examine the idea.
Bias: Attributing less mind and less capacity to suffer to the animals we eat.
Bias: Belittling people who act for moral reasons, because their conduct feels like an accusation.
Bias: Rejecting a proposal because it came from the other side.
Bias: Judging the message by who says it rather than by what it says.
Bias: Adopting a habit or an idea because many people around you do.
Bias: Many disagree in private but think everyone else agrees.
Bias: Sticking with the option that comes ready-made, like the plate with meat.

t: Illusory truth and mere exposure effects
s: Bias: What you hear often seems true, and what is familiar seems better.
Bias: Judging as less serious the harm we don't cause with our own hands, or that results from not acting.
Bias: Seeing purpose and intention in nature: animals would "exist for" something.
Bias: The more victims, the less we feel for each; one identifiable victim moves us more than millions.

t: Loss aversion and the endowment effect
s: Bias: Losing what you have weighs more than gaining something equivalent.
Bias: Carrying on because you've invested a lot, not because it's worth it.
Bias: Remembering the past as better than it was.
Bias: People who know little about a topic tend to overestimate what they know.

t: Naive realism and the bias blind spot
s: Bias: Thinking we see the world as it is and only others are biased.
Bias: Using humans as the measure of everything, including of what counts as feeling.
Bias: What seems natural is judged better and safer.
Bias: Judging by the easiest memory, like an acquaintance's case, rather than by the data.
Bias: Accepting a claim because of the prestige of whoever makes it.
Bias: Giving too much weight to now and too little to future consequences.
Bias: One good quality, like "local" or "organic", colors the judgment of everything else.
Bias: Preferring hierarchies between groups, including between species.
Bias: Believing each kind of being has a fixed essence that defines its place.
Bias: Associating eating meat with manliness, which makes change feel like a threat to identity.
Bias: Judging someone by a simplified image of the group they belong to.
Bias: Separating the animal from the food, including through the words we use.
Bias: Overestimating how many people think like us.
Bias: Distrusting unfamiliar foods.
Bias: Expecting something to do harm produces real symptoms.
Bias: Giving weight to what grabs attention, like the distance traveled, rather than to what matters most.
Bias: Thinking the middle position is always the most sensible.
Bias: Feeling less empathy for an animal the more evolutionarily distant it is from us.
Bias: Giving an animal less importance because it is small.
Bias: Giving an animal less importance because it is seen as not very intelligent.
Bias: Giving a being less importance because of the material it is made of, as with non-organic beings.
Bias: Judging help by the fraction of the problem it solves rather than by the number of individuals helped.
Bias: Believing the world is fair, so those who suffer are getting what is due to them.
Bias: Deciding under uncertainty without weighing the probability, treating a risk as certain or as nonexistent.
Bias: Avoiding options whose chance of success is unknown, even when they may be the best ones.
Bias: Giving more weight to what is easy to measure than to what matters most.
Bias: Judging an experience by its striking moments and its end, without counting how long it lasted.
Bias: Overestimating what an innovation will solve and not seeing its limits.
Bias: Treating a probability as if it were zero or one instead of taking the uncertainty into account.
Bias: Holding on to a belief even after learning of evidence against it.
Bias: Information that has already been corrected keeps influencing what a person thinks.
Bias: Seeing a situation as a contest in which one side's gain is the other's loss, even when it is not.
Bias: An idea gains credit by being repeated a lot in public, and the more credit it gains, the more it is repeated.
Bias: Seeing a link between two things that merely happened together.
Bias: The same information leads to different judgments depending on how it is presented.
Bias: Thinking you understand how something works much better than you actually do.
